PortBench: A Correlation-Aware, Full-Pipeline Benchmark
for LLM-Driven Portfolio Management

Yuxuan Zhao Affiliation: Yantai Research Institute of Harbin Engineering University Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Sijia Chen Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Ningxin Su Email: sijiachen@hkust-gz.edu.cnProject page: https://portbench.github.io/ Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance across diverse financial tasks, yet portfolio management (PM) remains poorly evaluated. Existing benchmarks exhibit two gaps: they are often equity-only and ignore cross-asset correlations; they provide limited insight into where errors arise and how they affect subsequent decisions. We introduce PortBench, a benchmark with market data spanning six asset classes from 2015 to 2025. PortBench comprises a static QA dataset of 6,269 questions across seven task templates and a dynamic five-stage portfolio evaluation. Dynamic evaluation uses a class-level correlation score for allocation and CEPS to summarize reference-based stage scores. We further evaluate under three stress windows and three risk profiles, and support real-time evaluation on newly arriving market data. Evaluating ten LLMs reveals a disconnect: high financial QA scores do not ensure consistent portfolio outperformance. LLMs concentrate exposure in correlated assets, and their portfolios achieve higher Sharpe than equal weighting in 54.2% of 120 evaluations across four market periods. Our source code is available at this https URL.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing capabilities across diverse financial tasks, spurring benchmarks for financial knowledge, numerical reasoning, and investment decision-making (Chen et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025b; Tang et al., 2025). Portfolio management (PM), however, remains inadequately evaluated. PM requires diversified allocations to reduce volatility and risk, which in turn requires accounting for intra- and inter-class correlations (Markowitz, 1952; Qian, 2005). Investment decisions put capital at risk. Assessing the reliability of PM systems therefore requires evaluating each stage and how its errors affect later decisions.

However, existing financial benchmarks fail to comprehensively evaluate PM due to two gaps. First, they often restrict coverage to a single asset class (Liu et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025a; Oh et al., 2025); even in multi-asset settings, assets are evaluated in isolation (Li et al., 2025b), which ignores cross-asset correlation structures. This design fails to distinguish between highly concentrated portfolios and genuinely diversified ones, even when their returns are identical. Additionally, LLM-based multi-agent systems for portfolio construction are consistently evaluated on equities alone with proprietary backtests that differ in data period, stock pools, and metrics, making cross-method comparison infeasible (Yu et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025a).

Second, existing benchmarks provide limited diagnosis of the investment decision process. Most financial benchmarks rely on static QA that probes knowledge without linking answers to realistic allocation (Xie et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025). The few that test portfolio decisions use single-step predictions or cover only part of the workflow (Chen et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2025; Saha et al., 2025); none spans the full cycle of market interpretation, signal generation, weight optimization, execution, and risk monitoring. These evaluations leave unclear where errors arise and how they affect subsequent decisions. Most further assume one implicit risk profile in normal markets, leaving the resilience of PM strategies under stress and alignment with investor-specific risk tolerances largely untested (Chen et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026a).

To address these gaps, we introduce PortBench, a benchmark for LLM-driven PM with market data spanning six asset classes from 2015 to 2025. PortBench evaluates LLMs through two complementary layers: a static QA dataset probing financial reasoning, and a dynamic five-stage sandbox that evaluates decisions at each stage of the PM cycle under sequential market conditions. Beyond historical replay, PortBench also supports real-time evaluation on up-to-date market data. Figure 1 provides an overview. Our contributions are:

  • •

    A Multi-Asset Market Dataset. We construct a 2015–2025 corpus of 183 market series across six asset classes, with prices, macro series, and time-aligned news, enabling correlation-aware PM evaluation beyond single-asset settings.

  • •

    A Dual-Layer Evaluation Framework. We pair static QA with a five-stage pipeline to evaluate financial reasoning and its use in portfolio decisions. Within the pipeline, CEPS summarizes reference-based stage scores, while paired interventions trace how local changes affect later decisions. We then evaluate the resulting portfolios across historical stress windows and investor profiles, with real-time evaluation extending coverage beyond historical replay.

  • •

    A QA–Portfolio Performance Gap. Across the ten evaluated LLMs, high financial QA scores do not ensure consistent portfolio outperformance. Models concentrate exposure in correlated assets, and their portfolios beat equal weighting on Sharpe in 54.2% of 120 evaluations across four historical market periods.

2 PortBench

2.1 Benchmark Construction

We construct the market base dataset, covering six asset classes: equities (126 tickers), commodities (16 tickers), bonds (15 series), cryptocurrency (12 tickers), real estate (10 series), and cash equivalents (4 series). In total, the dataset comprises 183 market series spanning January 2015 through December 2025. For each instrument, we collect daily price histories, return series, and associated news text; macroeconomic indicators include interest rates, inflation measures, credit spreads, and volatility indices. Stress windows are drawn from within this range and do not overlap with the normal period. Correlation analysis of the market base dataset reveals that inter-class average correlations are generally low, while intra-class correlations are strongly positive; see Appendix B for details.

2.2 Evaluation Framework

Building on the market base dataset, PortBench evaluates LLMs through two complementary layers, as illustrated in Figure 2.

QA evaluation. In the static layer, 6,269 QA pairs are generated across seven task templates spanning four complexity levels (L1–L4), probing financial reasoning abilities from single-asset prediction and sizing (L1: T1–T3) through pairwise allocation (L2: T4) and constrained multi-asset optimization (L3: T5–T6) to regime-driven judgment (L4: T7). Automated generation from historical data enables scalable template additions and dataset regeneration without manual annotation. Representative QA samples are in Appendix H.2.

Dynamic evaluation. The market base dataset is replayed point-in-time across the evaluation window. At each rebalance, the model receives a market snapshot and sequentially produces S1 (Market Interpretation), which assigns sentiment scores and identifies the prevailing regime; S2 (Signal Generation), which maps these views to directional signals; and S3 (Weight Optimization), which proposes portfolio weights. The sandbox executes the S3 allocation under fixed transaction costs. S4 (Execution Simulation) scores turnover agreement with the reference, while S5 (Risk Monitoring) compares lookback VaR, drawdown, and a rule-based rebalance flag computed from the proposed and reference allocations. Both deterministically evaluate S3 under identical execution and risk rules across models. A stateful sandbox records stage scores, proposed weights, and the resulting NAV trajectory, linking allocations to realized costs, returns, and risk under a common execution policy. Beyond historical replay, PortBench supports real-time evaluation on recent market data. Appendix C details evaluation and replay; Appendix H shows snapshots and full pipeline traces.

Pipeline metrics. CEPS summarizes reference-based stage scores with a penalty for downstream score drops. Let σt∈[0,1]\sigma_{t}\in[0,1] denote the normalized score at pipeline stage t∈{1,…,5}t\in\{1,\ldots,5\}, and let σ¯=15​∑t=15σt\bar{\sigma}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{t=1}^{5}\sigma_{t} be the mean stage score. With cascade penalty weight λ=0.1\lambda=0.1, CEPS =clip⁡(σ¯−λ​∑t=14max⁡(σt−σt+1, 0), 0, 1)\text{CEPS }=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\bar{\sigma}-\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{4}\max(\sigma_{t}-\sigma_{t+1},\ 0),\ 0,\ 1\right). At the same mean score, CEPS assigns a lower value to a pipeline with larger downstream drops, penalizing higher upstream scores followed by lower downstream scores. For S3, we combine reference-weight similarity with class-level correlation structure: σ3=α​sacc​(𝐰,𝐰∗)+(1−α)​scorr​(𝐰)\sigma_{3}=\alpha\,s_{\text{acc}}(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{w}^{*})+(1-\alpha)\,s_{\text{corr}}(\mathbf{w}), with α=0.5\alpha=0.5. Here sacc​(𝐰,𝐰∗)=1−12​∑i|wi−wi∗|s_{\text{acc}}(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{w}^{*})=1-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}|w_{i}-w_{i}^{*}| measures total-variation proximity to a signal- and profile-constrained reference allocation 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} estimated from the lookback window, while scorrs_{\text{corr}} combines exposure to internally correlated classes with cross-class hedging. The lookback reference supplies a reproducible decision-time target; returns and risk are evaluated from the resulting portfolios. Asset-level covariance analysis complements the class-level score by testing how within-class weighting affects portfolio risk at fixed asset selection and class exposure, see Section 4.2 for details. Appendix C.2 defines the scores, and Appendix F.6 examines ranking sensitivity to λ\lambda and α\alpha.

Paired stage interventions. To measure downstream effects, PortBench replaces one stage output with its reference output, reruns the subsequent stages, and compares their scores with the original branch. This auxiliary diagnostic scores generated S4/S5 plans; the main ranking scores turnover and lookback risk-state agreement (Appendix F.8).

Stress windows and investor profiles. We report normal-period CEPS with a stress drawdown gate under three historical windows (2015 China Shock, 2020 COVID Crash, 2022 Market Decline), and across three investor profiles (conservative, balanced, aggressive) whose exposure and drawdown constraints condition the S1/S2 prompts and their resulting signals. We compare matched allocations and realized returns and risk across profiles. Appendix C.3 gives profile limits and gate criteria.

3 Experiments

3.1 Experimental Setup

LLMs. We evaluate ten frontier LLMs: Kimi-K2.6 (Kimi Team, 2026), Qwen3.7-Max (Qwen Team, 2026c), Qwen3.6-Plus (Qwen Team, 2026b), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a), GLM-5.1 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), Doubao-Seed-2.0-Lite and Doubao-Seed-2.0-Pro (DB-2.0-Lite/Pro) (ByteDance Seed, 2026), Hunyuan3-Preview (HY3-Preview) (Tencent Hy Team, 2026), and DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DS-V4-Flash/Pro) (DeepSeek-ai, 2026).

Evaluation Protocol. We set the temperature to 0 and maximum output length to 8192 tokens, with thinking mode enabled by default. For static QA, each model answers the same 50 test questions per template using zero-shot prompting. For dynamic evaluation, models produce S1–S3 outputs and are evaluated through the five-stage pipeline under three investor profiles, using monthly decisions in the normal period and weekly decisions during stress windows to capture portfolio responses to rapidly changing market conditions. We use a 2024 bull-market window as the normal period and three historical stress windows for the stress gate and cross-period Sharpe comparisons. All strategies use the same eligible assets, next-close execution, and transaction costs; see Appendix C for details.

Baselines. We compare LLM-driven portfolios against six classical strategies: (1) Equal-Weight (EqW, 1/n1/n) allocates capital uniformly across assets; (2) 60/40 allocates 60% to equities and 40% to bonds; (3) Risk Parity (RiskPar) weights assets inversely to volatility; (4) Covariance Risk Parity (CovRiskPar) extends RiskPar using the full covariance matrix for equal risk contribution; (5) Minimum Variance (MinVar) selects the long-only portfolio on the Markowitz efficient frontier that minimizes variance (Markowitz, 1952); (6) Black–Litterman (BL) blends prior returns with simple views. These strategies retain their standard rules across profiles and are evaluated on Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, volatility, and total return.

3.2 Static QA Evaluation

Portfolio QA performance is task-dependent: models excel at formula-based allocation but remain weak on prediction and rebalancing. Table 1 shows that eight of ten models exceed 0.94 on T3; six score 1.00 on T4, and all reach at least 0.956. In contrast, none exceeds 0.520 on return prediction (T1), while rebalancing scores (T6) range from 0.468 to 0.882. T4–T5 (allocation with supplied covariance statistics) average 0.863, versus 0.652 for T1–T2 and T6–T7 (prediction, risk estimation, rebalancing, and regime detection); this 0.211 gap favors T4–T5 for eight of ten models (Appendix D.4). Supplementary structured T3/T4 tasks show that several LLMs retain near-ceiling performance on position-sizing and allocation-constraint reasoning, with details in Appendix D.3.

3.3 Pipeline Evaluation

Similar allocation scores conceal downstream differences. Table 2 ranks GLM-5.1 first and Qwen3.6-Plus second by CEPS under all three profiles. Across the 30 model–profile combinations, S1 ranges from .742 to .807 and S3 from only .264 to .310, while turnover agreement (S4) spans .121–.320 and risk-state agreement (S5) .000–.409. Under the conservative profile, Qwen3.6-Plus outperforms GLM-5.1 at four of five stages, but GLM-5.1’s S4 score is nearly twice as high (.304 vs. .153), yielding a slightly higher CEPS (.299 vs. .292). Similar allocation scores can therefore mask differences in turnover and risk-state agreement that affect overall pipeline rankings.

Normal-period drawdown rankings can reverse under stress. In the normal period, 15 of the 30 model–profile cells outperform EqW on Sharpe, and all 30 remain within their respective drawdown limits. Figure 3 shows that all ten models fail at least one conservative-profile scenario; nine pass all three balanced-profile scenarios and all ten pass the aggressive-profile scenarios. Under the balanced profile, DS-V4-Flash moves from the smallest normal-period drawdown (6.56%) to the largest COVID-window drawdown (22.19%), becoming the only model to fail that profile’s stress gate. Low normal-market drawdown therefore does not establish stress resilience. Details are in Appendix E.1.

3.4 QA–Pipeline Rank Inversion

QA and pipeline rankings differ sharply. GLM-5.1 moves from seventh in QA to first in balanced-profile CEPS, Kimi-K2.6 from last to fourth, and DS-V4-Flash from tied first to tenth (ρ=−.32\rho=-.32). Direct QA–Sharpe correlations across ten models range from −.67-.67 to +.83+.83 over the twelve period–profile settings. Positive associations appear in conservative and balanced 2015–16 settings, while the other ten intervals include zero (Appendix D.5). The observed QA rankings do not consistently carry over to portfolio outcomes.

Dynamic allocation requires combining market interpretation, signals, and profile constraints over the portfolio. T4/T5 test allocation with supplied statistics. Appendix D examines task scores through information ablations and supplementary structured decisions. Dynamic evaluation tests how local answers are used in portfolio construction, which standalone QA does not establish.

3.5 Cross-Period Evaluation

To probe performance under diverse market conditions, we reuse the three stress windows and report period Sharpe under three investor profiles: 2015–16 (volatile), 2020 (COVID crash and rebound), and 2022 (bear), alongside 2024 (bull). Across the 120 evaluated model–profile–period cases, LLMs beat EqW in 65 cases (54.2%). Figure 4 plots Sharpe minus EqW for every model–profile pair. Beat rates vary sharply: 77% in the 2020 crash-and-rebound window, 90% in 2015–16, 50% in the 2024 bull market, and 0% in the prolonged 2022 bear market. EqW Sharpe is -0.602 in 2020, where the mean model gap is +0.68+0.68, but reaches 0.710 in 2024; in 2022, every model–profile pair trails EqW, with mean Δ\DeltaSharpe −0.74-0.74. LLM portfolios show no consistent Sharpe advantage over EqW across these four windows. Across fixed model–profile pairs, the mean range of Δ\DeltaSharpe over the four periods is 1.84, compared with .71 across profiles within the same model and period, showing that relative performance varies more across these market-window and decision-frequency settings than across investor profiles. Appendices E.2 and E.3 report results and NAV trajectories.

3.6 Real-Time Evaluation

Evaluating historical markets risks leakage from prices, headlines, or outcomes seen during LLM pretraining (Li et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025a). PortBench therefore supports real-time evaluation with point-in-time inputs: at each decision date, the model receives only data available through the previous close and runs the five-stage pipeline. Over 12 trading days (2026-07-16–07-31), we collect 72 decisions from six models with daily rebalancing. Mean S1 scores range from .78 to .82, while S4 turnover agreement remains low at .047–.163. This initial run demonstrates stage-level evaluation on newly arriving data and more frequent portfolio decisions. Appendix G reports daily stage scores and lookback CEPS.

4 Deep Analysis

4.1 Local Gains Can Fade or Reverse

Paired interventions under the balanced profile test how replacing one stage with its reference affects later decisions. In this auxiliary diagnostic, S4/S5 score the model’s execution and risk-management plans. Replacing S1 with its reference output raises S2 by +.626+.626 in normal episodes; both references follow the same trailing-return rule. Its mean effect on S3 is only +.017+.017 and is negative in 40 of 110 episodes. Replacing S2 raises S3 by only +.023+.023, with 39 negative cases. Under stress, S2 and S3 replacement reduce S5 by −.059-.059 and −.056-.056, although most episode-level S5 changes are zero. Large gains at the next stage become much smaller or turn negative at later stages. Case traces reveal execution and risk changes missed by stage scores; see Appendix F.8 for details.

4.2 Broad Holdings Conceal Correlated Risk

The 330 saved 2024-normal allocations hold 73 assets on average, yet still concentrate weight in correlated assets. For each decision, we construct a matched allocation by equalizing weights among held assets within each class while preserving asset selection, class weights, and uninvested cash. This isolates the risk effect of within-class weights.

Across ten models, three profiles, and eleven decision dates, this equalization lowers volatility estimated from lookback data by 8.5% on average, with reductions in 271/330 decisions. Figure 5A shows higher volatility-weighted pairwise correlation under model weights for all models. Panel B attributes 76.4% of the mean variance difference to within-class covariance, versus 23.5% to individual-asset variance terms. Panel C shows larger mean volatility reductions under more aggressive profiles: 1.6%, 9.6%, and 14.4% for conservative, balanced, and aggressive allocations. Diversification depends on how capital is distributed among correlated holdings, even when asset selections and class exposures are unchanged. Appendix F.9 gives the covariance decomposition, model–profile results, and sensitivity analyses.

Active allocation and realized risk.

Across the 30 cells, the mean total-variation distance is 0.306 from EqW and 0.890 from the profile-constrained reference. Figure 6 relates distance from EqW to realized outcomes. Larger deviations from EqW are associated with higher volatility (ρ=.65\rho=.65), drawdown magnitude (ρ=.61\rho=.61), and Δ\DeltaSharpe (ρ=.51\rho=.51) in the normal period. The models therefore take meaningful active positions, with higher relative Sharpe accompanied by greater volatility and drawdowns (DeMiguel et al., 2009). Moving from conservative to aggressive increases distance from EqW by .070 on matched allocations.

Allocation-to-execution gap.

Under the balanced profile, every model produces less turnover than the reference; overall, the mean model-to-reference turnover ratio is .203. Reference allocations hold 8–14 securities, with maximum weights of .24–.72, whereas model allocations spread weight more broadly. Total-variation distance from the reference averages .890, giving mean S3 reference-weight similarity of .110. Mean model HHI is .0207, whose reciprocal is about 48 effective positions. The allocations differ from the reference in both concentration and turnover, explaining why partial credit for class exposure can coexist with low S4 scores. Appendix F.4 reports the diagnostics; Appendix H.3 gives full traces.

4.3 Performance Reverses across Regimes

In 2020, 23 of 30 cases beat EqW, whereas none do so in 2022. Both windows use weekly decisions, contrasting a sharp crash and recovery with a prolonged decline. EqW’s Sharpe is similar in these windows (−.602-.602 versus −.540-.540), whereas mean model Sharpe falls from .074.074 to −1.281-1.281. The reversal therefore reflects changes in model-portfolio performance, rather than simply a stronger benchmark. The mean relative Sharpe advantage is largest in the crash-and-rebound window. The mean Sharpe advantage of aggressive over conservative profiles is largest in 2020 at +.935+.935, compared with −.039-.039 in 2022 and +.214+.214 in 2024 (Appendix E.2); details are in Appendix F.7.

4.4 Risk Profiles Shift Exposure

On matched model–date pairs, shifting from conservative to aggressive raises risk-asset exposure by .175 and lowers bond-plus-cash exposure by .162. Normal-period volatility rises by .050 for nine of ten models and drawdown magnitude by .047 for eight. Mean Sharpe increases by .214, with nine improving and one declining. Under stress, the shift raises volatility for all ten in 2020 and 2022. Yet total return rises for all ten in the 2020 rebound and falls for nine in the 2022 decline. In 2022, five models achieve higher Sharpe under the aggressive profile, yet four have lower returns and deeper drawdowns. With negative excess returns, higher volatility can make Sharpe less negative, highlighting the need to assess returns and drawdowns alongside Sharpe. Profiles change exposure, risk, and normal-period returns, while the return advantage varies across periods. Figure 5C shows more scope to reduce estimated volatility in aggressive portfolios through within-class reweighting without changing asset selections or class exposures. Appendix F.5 reports matched changes.

5 Related Work

Financial LLM benchmarks have progressed from knowledge retrieval (Chen et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2023) to investment decision-making (Xie et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Luo et al., 2025a), yet portfolio management evaluations remain limited to static QA, single-asset-class backtests, or asset-by-asset backtests (Liu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025b). StockBench (Chen et al., 2025a) introduces process-level analysis but lacks cross-asset correlation scoring and investor-profile adaptation; LLM agents for PM (Yu et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025d) rely on proprietary backtests that assess only terminal outcomes (Chen et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026a). Despite robust portfolio construction relying on covariance structures (Markowitz, 1952; Qian, 2005) and non-LLM methods exploiting them (Zhang et al., 2025a), cross-asset correlation risk remains underexamined in LLM portfolio evaluation (Chen et al., 2025c). PortBench examines how multi-asset allocation decisions translate into portfolio risk across market regimes and investor profiles. Full discussion is in Appendix A.

6 Conclusion

We presented PortBench, a benchmark for LLM-driven portfolio management with market data spanning six asset classes from 2015 to 2025. PortBench provides a multi-asset market dataset of 183 market series with prices, macro series, and time-aligned news, alongside a dual-layer evaluation framework combining static PM QA with a five-stage evaluation of historical portfolios. The framework uses a class-level correlation metric, asset-level covariance diagnostics, and CEPS, and supports stress-window, investor-profile, and real-time evaluation. Despite high financial QA scores, the evaluated LLMs fail to beat equal weighting on Sharpe in 55 of 120 evaluations across four historical periods. Their portfolios hold many assets, yet within-class weights concentrate exposure in correlated holdings, limiting diversification. These findings expose a gap between financial QA and portfolio performance: LLMs concentrate correlated exposures and show no consistent Sharpe advantage over equal weighting across these periods.

Limitations

Although PortBench provides a comprehensive evaluation framework, several limitations remain: (1) The sandbox environment relies on deterministic transaction costs applied to historical price data, so it does not capture real-world microstructure dynamics, liquidity constraints, and order-flow impact. Integrating generative market simulators like MarS (Li et al., 2025c) to model tokenized order flow and support shock injection would provide more realistic execution feedback. (2) Historical evaluation uses monthly decisions in the normal period and weekly decisions in three selected stress windows. The daily real-time window covers twelve trading days (Appendix G); longer real-time evaluation would help test whether the results hold across periods. (3) The model produces S1–S3 through a fixed set of isolated LLM prompts without persistent memory, external tool access, or multi-agent coordination; the sandbox then computes the S4/S5 execution and risk scores used in the ranking from the S3 allocation (Xiao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025d). Future work should adopt agentic methods that incorporate tool calling, long-horizon memory, and inter-agent communication to improve portfolio management.

Ethical Statement

PortBench is designed as a research benchmark for evaluating LLM capabilities in portfolio management and is not intended as financial advice or as a decision-support tool for real investment. All evaluations use publicly available historical market data; no proprietary, private, or personally identifiable information is used. The benchmark does not involve human subjects, and no crowd-sourced annotations were collected. We caution against deploying LLM-generated portfolio allocations in live trading without rigorous human oversight. As our experiments demonstrate, the evaluated models fail to consistently outperform simple heuristic baselines and exhibit fragile behavior under stress conditions. The benchmark’s stress-test evaluation is specifically designed to surface such failure modes before deployment, but passing the stress gate does not certify safety in real-world use.

LLM Statement

We used LLM-based tools to polish the writing and refine the language of this paper.

Appendix A Additional Related Work

A.1 Financial LLM Benchmarks

Financial LLM benchmarks span knowledge retrieval, numerical reasoning, and quantitative tasks (Chen et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Shah et al., 2022; Islam et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Luo et al., 2025a; Gan et al., 2025). Most QA benchmarks stop before allocation under realized markets. Dynamic evaluations commonly restrict the asset universe to equities or cryptocurrencies (Liu et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025a; Oh et al., 2025), or score products independently instead of a joint portfolio (Li et al., 2025b). StockBench (Chen et al., 2025a) evaluates multiple trading steps for 20 DJIA equities, but omits cross-asset allocation and investor profiles. Table 3 compares PortBench on financial QA, joint multi-asset allocation, linked decisions, realized risk, and investor constraints.

A.2 LLMs in Financial Decision-Making

LLM agents now support market analysis, signal generation, and portfolio construction (Zhang et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Saha et al., 2025). FinCon (Yu et al., 2024) uses a manager–analyst hierarchy, MASS (Guo et al., 2025a) scales multi-agent portfolio simulation, HedgeAgents (Li et al., 2025d) assigns hedging specialists across asset classes, and a cryptocurrency framework (Luo et al., 2025b) coordinates agents over the top-30 cryptocurrencies. These systems are evaluated in separate backtesting settings. PortBench supplies one six-class market interface and scores each stage of a shared five-stage process, enabling stage-level comparison alongside portfolio outcomes.

A.3 Portfolio Risk Evaluation

Portfolio theory makes covariance central to allocation: modern portfolio theory (Markowitz, 1952) and risk parity (Qian, 2005) optimize portfolio-level variance or risk contributions. Data-driven methods also use cross-asset co-movement and temporal structure (Mantegna, 1999; Wang et al., 2021; Jeon et al., 2024); SmartFolio (Zhang et al., 2025a), for example, penalizes positive intra-class correlation and rewards inter-class hedging. Risk-first evaluation further shows why average returns alone miss failures under market stress (Chen et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025c). PortBench addresses both requirements with correlation-aware allocation scoring, three stress windows, and three investor profiles.

Appendix B Dataset and Market Context

PortBench covers 183 market series spanning 2015–2025 across six asset classes, collected from Yahoo Finance (price/return series), FRED (macroeconomic indicators), and Kaggle (supplementary equity and cryptocurrency series). Figure 7 shows instrument counts by asset class. Equities exhibit the broadest coverage (126 series), including individual stocks, broad-market, sector, and factor ETFs, and index context. Commodities (16 tickers) and bonds (15 series) provide representative cross-class hedging opportunities, cryptocurrency (12 tickers) captures major and mid-cap digital assets, and real estate (10 series) and cash equivalents (4 series) extend the market coverage.

Code and source data.

The benchmark implementation is licensed under Apache 2.0. Market data are obtained from the providers listed above, with reuse subject to the respective source terms. Historical allocation results use the evaluation subset defined in Appendix C.4.

Market context at decision time.

At each decision date, the model receives a point-in-time market context containing a 60-trading-day lookback window of price history and daily returns for all assets in scope; macro indicators (Fed funds rate, VIX, yield curve slope); an intra-class correlation matrix for each asset class and an inter-class correlation matrix, both recomputed from the lookback window at each decision date; any available news text or earnings filings preceding the decision date; the current portfolio weights; and the current portfolio NAV. The intra- and inter-class correlation matrices are formatted as structured tables and injected directly into the S1 and S3 prompts, giving models explicit access to the correlation information required for correlation-aware allocation. The correlation interface is restricted to the asset classes present in each snapshot.

B.1 Price Trajectories

Figure 8 displays representative market series from the six asset classes over 2015–2025. Coverage ranges from 126 equity instruments to four cash-related series. Within-class paths also differ: natural gas and crude oil fluctuate more sharply than gold, while BTC, SOL, BNB, DOT, and AVAX follow distinct cryptocurrency cycles and listing histories. These series differ in history length, volatility, and drawdown patterns. The dataset combines long-history traditional assets with later-listed cryptocurrencies, so history lengths differ across assets in the dataset.

B.2 Data Preprocessing

Calendar alignment.

All price and return series are aligned to a common business-day calendar. For realized portfolio accounting, short price gaps of up to five consecutive trading days are forward-filled before computing returns; daily returns are not carried forward. Gaps exceeding five days are retained as missing values and excluded from correlation estimation using pairwise complete observations, so that assets with non-overlapping listing histories (particularly cryptocurrency) do not reduce the effective sample for other asset pairs.

Market regime labeling.

Each asset class is assigned one of four market regime labels, bull, bear, sideways, or crisis, on a rolling basis. A crisis window begins when the maximum drawdown from the trailing 252-trading-day peak exceeds 15%. Bull and bear periods are identified using a dual moving-average crossover rule (50-day and 200-day); periods where neither condition is satisfied are labeled sideways. Regime labels group QA samples and evaluation results by market regime.

Data splits.

The dataset is divided into three non-overlapping splits with year-end boundaries:

  • •

    Train: 2015–2022 (eight years; used for correlation matrix estimation and QA generation)

  • •

    Validation: 2023 (one year; used for hyperparameter selection and QA validation)

  • •

    Test: 2024–2025 (two years; held out for reported QA evaluation)

Pipeline evaluation uses calendar windows that sit inside this coverage but serve a different role: the primary normal-period backtest is the 2024 bull window, with 2015–16, 2020, and 2022 reserved for stress-gate and cross-period Sharpe comparisons (Section 3). These pipeline windows are therefore evaluation regimes, not a redefinition of the QA train/val/test split.

Correlation matrix estimation.

Figures 9 and 10 use a dataset-level Pearson matrix computed from 2015–2022 daily returns with pairwise complete observations. Each pipeline episode recomputes its correlation matrix from the trailing 60 trading days available at the decision date. The profile-constrained S3 reference, CovRiskPar, MinVar, and Black–Litterman use covariance estimated from the same decision-time snapshot; covariance-based baselines apply 252-day annualization. Pearson correlation maps directly to the intra- and inter-class scoring formulas in Appendix C.2.

B.3 Correlation Structure

Figures 9 and 10 show low average correlation for several cross-class pairs and stronger positive correlation within equities and real estate. Diversification depends on which asset classes receive weight: spreading capital inside a highly correlated class provides less hedging than allocating across weakly correlated classes.

Appendix C Evaluation Protocol

C.1 QA Task Templates

QA targets are generated automatically from the market base dataset and explicit task definitions, without manual item-level annotation. They include realized outcomes (T1), numerical calculations and decision rules (T2–T6), and a predefined regime-to-allocation policy (T7).

QA results report mean task scores in [0,1][0,1]. T1 uses exact direction-label agreement. T2/T3 use max⁡(0,1−|y^−y|/|y|)\max(0,1-|\hat{y}-y|/|y|) for nonzero numeric targets; a zero target receives one only when |y^|<10−6|\hat{y}|<10^{-6}. T4/T5 use cosine similarity between predicted and target weight vectors. T6/T7 use the component scores defined below. Missing or unparseable answers receive zero, and the overall QA score averages the seven template means equally.

T1 (Return direction). The ground truth is the sign of the realized hh-day forward return, where hh is the forecast horizon specified in the question (default h=21h{=}21 trading days). Direction labels are positive, negative, or flat (within ±1%\pm 1\%).

T2 (VaR estimation). Historical simulation VaR at confidence level pp (e.g., p=0.95p{=}0.95 or 0.990.99; distinct from the S3 mixing weight α\alpha):

VaRp=quantile(r1:L, 1−p)\text{VaR}_{p}=\text{quantile}(r_{1:L},\;1-p)

where r1:Lr_{1:L} is the trailing lookback return series provided in the question (default L=60L{=}60 trading days). The scored answer is VaRp\text{VaR}_{p}; the question specifies the requested confidence level.

T3 (Position sizing). The fixed-fractional Kelly-inspired formula (Kelly, 1956):

f∗=min⁡(1.0,δmax|VaR99%|)f^{*}=\min\!\left(1.0,\;\frac{\delta_{\text{max}}}{|\text{VaR}_{99\%}|}\right)

where δmax\delta_{\text{max}} is the question’s drawdown limit.

T4 (Long-only minimum-variance pairwise allocation). The prompt includes individual daily volatilities ς1\varsigma_{1}, ς2\varsigma_{2} (distinct from pipeline stage scores σt\sigma_{t}), annualized mean returns μ1\mu_{1}, μ2\mu_{2}, and a minimum annualized portfolio return μmin\mu_{\min}. The full condition also provides the pairwise daily covariance and correlation; the restricted condition in Section D.4 removes these two statistics. The target minimizes two-asset variance subject to the stated return floor:

minw1,w2\displaystyle\min_{w_{1},w_{2}}\quad w12​ς12+w22​ς22+2​w1​w2​ς12\displaystyle w_{1}^{2}\varsigma_{1}^{2}+w_{2}^{2}\varsigma_{2}^{2}+2w_{1}w_{2}\varsigma_{12}
s.t. w1+w2=1,w1,w2≥0,\displaystyle w_{1}+w_{2}=1,\quad w_{1},w_{2}\geq 0,
w1​μ1+w2​μ2≥μmin,\displaystyle w_{1}\mu_{1}+w_{2}\mu_{2}\geq\mu_{\min},

where ς12\varsigma_{12} is the lookback sample covariance. Without a binding return floor, the long-only minimum-variance target is w1=clip⁡((ς22−ς12)/(ς12+ς22−2​ς12),0,1)w_{1}=\operatorname{clip}((\varsigma_{2}^{2}-\varsigma_{12})/(\varsigma_{1}^{2}+\varsigma_{2}^{2}-2\varsigma_{12}),0,1) and w2=1−w1w_{2}=1-w_{1}; a vanishing denominator uses equal weights. When the floor binds, the weights satisfy w1​μ1+w2​μ2=μminw_{1}\mu_{1}+w_{2}\mu_{2}=\mu_{\min}, giving w1=(μmin−μ2)/(μ1−μ2)w_{1}=(\mu_{\min}-\mu_{2})/(\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}) and w2=1−w1w_{2}=1-w_{1}.

T5 (Maximum-Sharpe allocation). The long-only maximum-Sharpe portfolio for three or more assets, solved numerically via constrained optimization:

max𝐰⁡𝐰⊤​𝝁−rf𝐰⊤​𝚺​𝐰s.t.∑iwi=1,wi≥0\max_{\mathbf{w}}\frac{\mathbf{w}^{\top}\bm{\mu}-r_{f}}{\sqrt{\mathbf{w}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}}}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\textstyle\sum_{i}w_{i}=1,\;w_{i}\geq 0

with a risk-free rate of rf=4%r_{f}=4\% per annum and annualized 𝝁\bm{\mu}, 𝚺\bm{\Sigma} estimated from the 60-day lookback window. The pipeline S3 reference in Appendix C.2 uses the raw sample mean and covariance without rfr_{f}. Equal weight is used as a fallback if the optimizer does not converge. Under the full condition the prompt includes the full mean vector 𝝁\bm{\mu} and covariance matrix 𝚺\bm{\Sigma}; under the restricted condition the covariance matrix and its header row are stripped (see Section D.4).

T6 (Rebalancing decision with trade specification). The model is presented with a holdings table of current weights and target weights; pre-computed deviations are withheld. The ground truth is determined as follows. Let i∗=arg​maxi⁡|wicurrent−witarget|i^{*}=\operatorname{arg\,max}_{i}|w_{i}^{\text{current}}-w_{i}^{\text{target}}| be the most off-target asset. The rebalancing flag is:

rebalance=[|wi∗current−wi∗target|>δreb],\text{rebalance}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[|w_{i^{*}}^{\text{current}}-w_{i^{*}}^{\text{target}}|>\delta_{\text{reb}}\right],

with default threshold δreb=0.05\delta_{\text{reb}}=0.05 (distinct from the profile drawdown tolerance δdd\delta_{\text{dd}}). Classes are balanced by construction, with half of all instances requiring rebalancing and half not, yielding exactly 50% positive / 50% negative labels.

The answer has two parts. Part A: a yes/no rebalancing decision. Part B (required when Part A is yes): the corrective trade, expressed as “sell X.XXXX of ASSET” or “buy X.XXXX of ASSET”, where ASSET =i∗=i^{*} and the trade size is |wi∗current−wi∗target||w_{i^{*}}^{\text{current}}-w_{i^{*}}^{\text{target}}| (reported but not scored).

Scoring decomposes as follows. If the ground truth is no: score =1=1 if the model answers no, else 00. If the ground truth is yes: score =0.40×dyes+0.60×(0.50×cdir+0.50×casset)=0.40\times d_{\text{yes}}+0.60\times(0.50\times c_{\text{dir}}+0.50\times c_{\text{asset}}), where dyes=𝟏​[model answers yes]d_{\text{yes}}=\mathbf{1}[\text{model answers yes}], cdirc_{\text{dir}} indicates correct trade direction (buy versus sell), and cassetc_{\text{asset}} indicates correct asset identification.

T7 (Regime detection and allocation). The target regime is the label assigned to the decision date by the regime classifier. The allocation target uses a predefined mapping from each regime to an increase, decrease, or hold direction for each asset class. This mapping specifies the benchmark’s reference policy:

Regime EQ BO CO RE CR CA Bull ↑\uparrow ↓\downarrow ∼\sim ↑\uparrow ↑\uparrow ↓\downarrow Bear ↓\downarrow ↑\uparrow ∼\sim ↓\downarrow ↓\downarrow ↑\uparrow Sideways ∼\sim ∼\sim ∼\sim ∼\sim ↓\downarrow ↑\uparrow Crisis ↓\downarrow ↑\uparrow ↑\uparrow ↓\downarrow ↓\downarrow ↑\uparrow

EQ = equities, BO = bonds, CO = commodities, RE = real estate, CR = cryptocurrency, CA = cash. ↑\uparrow = increase, ↓\downarrow = decrease, ∼\sim = hold. Scoring is score=0.5dreg+0.51|𝒞|∑c∈𝒞𝟏[a^c=ac∗]\text{score}=0.5\,d_{\text{reg}}+0.5\,\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{a}_{c}=a_{c}^{*}], where dreg=𝟏[regime^=regime∗]d_{\text{reg}}=\mathbf{1}[\widehat{\text{regime}}=\text{regime}^{*}], 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the set of six asset classes, and a^c\hat{a}_{c}, ac∗a_{c}^{*} are the predicted and ground-truth allocation directions for class cc.

C.2 Pipeline Metrics

Stage scores and CEPS.

Each stage has an explicit target. S1/S2 use trailing-return rules, S3 uses a profile-constrained numerical allocation and class exposure, and S4/S5 measure turnover and lookback risk-state agreement. For 𝝈∈[0,1]5\bm{\sigma}\in[0,1]^{5}, the Cross-Stage Error Propagation Score is

σ¯\displaystyle\bar{\sigma} =15​∑t=15σt,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{5}\sum_{t=1}^{5}\sigma_{t}, (1)
Δcascade\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{cascade}} =∑t=14max⁡(σt−σt+1,0),\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{4}\max(\sigma_{t}-\sigma_{t+1},0), (2)
CEPS\displaystyle\mathrm{CEPS} =clip⁡(σ¯−.1​Δcascade,0,1).\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}(\bar{\sigma}-.1\Delta_{\mathrm{cascade}},0,1). (3)

CEPS combines the mean reference-based stage score with a penalty for downstream score drops. The five stage scores receive equal weight in the mean. Paired interventions measure downstream responses to a reference replacement (Appendix F.8).

S1: market interpretation.

For eligible asset ii, let RilbR_{i}^{\mathrm{lb}} be its cumulative return over the last 60 available observations within the preceding 90 calendar days, through the decision date. The reference view and agreement score are

vi∗\displaystyle v_{i}^{*} =clip⁡(Rilb/.10,−1,1),\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}(R_{i}^{\mathrm{lb}}/.10,-1,1), (4)
σ1\displaystyle\sigma_{1} =1−12​n​∑i=1n|v^i−vi∗|.\displaystyle=1-\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\hat{v}_{i}-v_{i}^{*}|. (5)

Here v^i∈[−1,1]\hat{v}_{i}\in[-1,1] is the model view and nn is the eligible security count; an absent view is neutral. The target specifies a reproducible momentum interpretation of the lookback data.

S2: signal generation.

The reference maps vi∗>.2v_{i}^{*}>.2 to buy, vi∗<−.2v_{i}^{*}<-.2 to sell, and the remaining values to hold. For model signals s^i\hat{s}_{i}, agreement is

σ2=1n∑i=1n𝟏[s^i=si∗].\sigma_{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}[\hat{s}_{i}=s_{i}^{*}]. (6)

Missing signals receive no agreement credit.

Profile-constrained lookback reference.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} contain reference-buy assets, 𝒟\mathcal{D} the eligible bond and cash securities, and ℰ\mathcal{E} equity and cryptocurrency assets. For profile pp, the reference numerically maximizes

𝐰⊤​𝝁𝐰⊤​𝚺​𝐰+ϵ\displaystyle\frac{\mathbf{w}^{\top}\bm{\mu}}{\sqrt{\mathbf{w}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}+\epsilon}} (7)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t. } ∑iwi=1,wi≥0,\displaystyle\sum_{i}w_{i}=1,\quad w_{i}\geq 0,
wi=0(i∉ℬ∪𝒟),\displaystyle w_{i}=0\quad(i\notin\mathcal{B}\cup\mathcal{D}),
∑i∈ℰwi≤αp,∑i∈𝒟wi≥βp.\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}}w_{i}\leq\alpha_{p},\qquad\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}w_{i}\geq\beta_{p}.

The sample mean 𝝁\bm{\mu} and covariance 𝚺\bm{\Sigma} use common observed dates in the trailing window, with no risk-free adjustment; ϵ=10−10\epsilon=10^{-10} stabilizes the denominator. SLSQP starts from a feasible allocation, with tolerance 10−910^{-9} and at most 500 iterations. A solution is accepted only if the solver succeeds, satisfies the constraints, and matches or improves the initial objective; otherwise the feasible start is retained. Defensive securities remain eligible regardless of signal to implement the profile floor. Real estate follows its separate asset class and is not included in the equity cap.

We denote the resulting numerical reference by 𝐰p∗\mathbf{w}_{p}^{*}. It gives all models a common allocation target for each date and profile, using only past returns. The objective evaluates return relative to volatility within the lookback sample; subsequent net returns, drawdown, and the stress gate assess investment outcomes. Historical stage scores use this lookback reference. Appendix F.2 compares it with an ex-post reference constructed from subsequent realized returns.

S3: allocation agreement and class exposure.

For normalized long-only portfolios, including any uninvested cash, reference similarity is

sacc=1−12​∑i|wi−wp,i∗|.s_{\mathrm{acc}}=1-\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i}|w_{i}-w_{p,i}^{*}|. (8)

It equals one for identical allocations and zero for disjoint allocations. S3 combines this term and class exposure with equal weight. Let WcW_{c} be total exposure to class cc, ρ¯c\bar{\rho}_{c} the mean within-class off-diagonal correlation, and ρ⁡(c,c′)\rho(c,c^{\prime}) the mean correlation between its eligible security pairs:

sintra\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{intra}} =clip⁡(1−∑cWc​max⁡(ρ¯c,0),0,1),\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(1-\sum_{c}W_{c}\max(\bar{\rho}_{c},0),0,1\right), (9)
ρ¯cross\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{cross}} =∑c≠c′Wc​Wc′​ρ​(c,c′)∑c≠c′Wc​Wc′,\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{c\neq c^{\prime}}W_{c}W_{c^{\prime}}\rho(c,c^{\prime})}{\sum_{c\neq c^{\prime}}W_{c}W_{c^{\prime}}}, (10)
sinter\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{inter}} =clip⁡((1−ρ¯cross)/2,0,1),\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}\!\left((1-\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{cross}})/2,0,1\right), (11)
scorr\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{corr}} =12​(sintra+sinter).\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(s_{\mathrm{intra}}+s_{\mathrm{inter}}). (12)

With no positive cross-class weight product, sinter=.5s_{\mathrm{inter}}=.5. Uninvested cash contributes to cash-class exposure; class correlations use the eligible securities. These scores describe the class allocation. Redistributing weights inside a class leaves them unchanged, and with exactly two positive classes the cross-class weight product cancels.

Asset-level correlation risk.

Portfolio variance V⁡(𝐰)=𝐰⊤​𝚺​𝐰V(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} and the weighted pairwise correlation in Appendix F.9 use the actual security weights. The matched within-class allocation provides a controlled test: selected securities and class totals are identical, while covariance exposure can change. The class score describes how capital is split across asset classes; these asset-level measures assess the risk associated with the weights within each class.

S4: turnover agreement.

Let τ⁡(𝐮,𝐰)=∑i≠cash|wi−ui|\tau(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w})=\sum_{i\neq\mathrm{cash}}|w_{i}-u_{i}| be traded security weight from pre-trade weights 𝐮\mathbf{u}. Both the proposed and reference targets are compared from the same pre-trade state. With τ=τ⁡(𝐮,𝐰)\tau=\tau(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}) and τ∗=τ⁡(𝐮,𝐰p∗)\tau^{*}=\tau(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}_{p}^{*}),

σ4=1−|τ−τ∗|max⁡(τ,τ∗,10−4).\sigma_{4}=1-\frac{|\tau-\tau^{*}|}{\max(\tau,\tau^{*},10^{-4})}. (13)

Agreement peaks at matching turnover. Trading costs are reported separately as a financial outcome.

S5: lookback risk-state agreement.

Apply the target weights to common lookback returns and compute the 5th-percentile daily VaR and maximum drawdown, including initial wealth in the running peak. The rebalance flag is true when drawdown breaches the profile tolerance or the maximum deviation from security equal weighting exceeds .05. For model and reference flags b,b∗b,b^{*} and risk statistics,

eV\displaystyle e_{V} =|V−V∗|max⁡(|V∗|,10−6),\displaystyle=\frac{|V-V^{*}|}{\max(|V^{*}|,10^{-6})}, (14)
eD\displaystyle e_{D} =|D−D∗|max⁡(|D∗|,10−6),\displaystyle=\frac{|D-D^{*}|}{\max(|D^{*}|,10^{-6})}, (15)
σ5\displaystyle\sigma_{5} =12𝟏[b=b∗]+12clip(1−eV+eD2,0,1).\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}[b=b^{*}]+\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{clip}\!\left(1-\tfrac{e_{V}+e_{D}}{2},0,1\right). (16)

Here VV denotes VaR and DD drawdown in this equation. Smaller and larger risk statistics both reduce reference agreement; realized volatility, drawdown, and the stress gate independently assess portfolio risk. The profile VaR threshold is available for risk alerts and does not set the rebalance flag.

C.3 Stress Windows and Profiles

The weekly stress schedule resolves changes during rapidly evolving market conditions; monthly normal-period evaluation measures longer holding intervals. All comparison strategies, including EqW, share the schedule within each window, so their relative performance is compared at the same decision frequency. All three stress windows use weekly decisions, so the 2020–2022 reversal is observed at the same decision frequency. Comparisons with monthly decisions in 2024 also reflect a change in decision frequency. The stress gate passes when realized maximum drawdown magnitude is at most δp\delta_{p} in every stress window.

Profiles appear in the S1/S2 prompts; S3 uses the resulting signals and market statistics. Exposure compliance evaluates both target-weight inequalities in Table 5.

C.4 Baselines and Common Portfolio Replay

Tradable securities.

The benchmark comprises 183 market series spanning six asset classes, supporting portfolio QA, macroeconomic and news context, and broad market coverage. Portfolio evaluation supplies 99 series with matched price histories: 43 equities, 15 bonds, 16 commodities, 10 real-estate assets, 10 cryptocurrencies, 4 cash instruments, and VIX. VIX is a market indicator, and any weight assigned to it is held as uninvested cash. The other 98 series are the investable assets. The remaining 84 corpus series (82 equities and 2 cryptocurrencies) are excluded from portfolio allocation. At each decision date, an investable asset is eligible when its price is positive and at least 20 return observations are available over the preceding 90 calendar days. Weight assigned to an ineligible asset is held as uninvested cash and is not redistributed. All compared portfolios use this eligibility rule.

Execution and return accounting.

Every portfolio starts with unit NAV in cash and replays its archived target sequence. A decision is executed at the first observed market close strictly after its date. Existing positions accrue that date’s return before trading, and new positions earn subsequent returns. The calendar uses observed SPY trading dates. Outcomes use archived adjusted prices: Yahoo series for ETFs and the adjusted-close column of the NASDAQ-100 source for individual equities. Short price gaps are forward-filled for at most five trading dates before computing returns. Each dated return is applied once. Commission of 5 bps and slippage of 10 bps are charged on the absolute changes in security weights; transferring the cash balance has no additional fee. Holdings drift between trades. Costs are relative to initial NAV.

Sharpe uses (252​r¯−.04)/(252​sr)(252\bar{r}-.04)/(\sqrt{252}s_{r}) from the net daily portfolio returns, with a fixed 4% annual risk-free rate across windows. Volatility is 252​sr\sqrt{252}s_{r}, total return is terminal NAV minus one, and maximum drawdown includes initial NAV in the running maximum. Each window contains all ten models and three profiles. The 2,790 saved decisions remain in coverage and allocation records; 60 terminal decisions have no following execution close inside their windows, leaving 2,730 executed decisions for stage-score summaries. All 120 portfolio cells remain in financial comparisons. The 330 normal-period decisions all execute. For MinVar in 2024, the risk-free adjustment contributes −3.13-3.13 to Sharpe at 1.28% annualized volatility; cumulative trading costs are 0.76% of initial NAV.

Classical strategies.

EqW distributes capital across the eligible securities. The 60/40 baseline equally weights eligible equities within its 60% sleeve and eligible bonds within its 40% sleeve. RiskPar uses inverse volatility; CovRiskPar uses full-covariance equal risk contribution; MinVar uses long-only minimum variance; BL combines a return prior and directional views. Covariance-based strategies use the common observed trailing returns with 252-day annualization. These six strategies retain their standard allocation rules, providing fixed strategy comparators across investor profiles.

C.5 Statistical Analysis

Per-template QA means retain all 50 evaluated items for each model. The seven-template QA aggregate weights each template equally. QA–Sharpe correlations use ten paired model observations separately for each period and profile. CEPS–outcome associations likewise compare models within each profile. Percentile intervals use 10,000 paired model-bootstrap draws. For the covariance comparisons, the model is the resampling cluster, retaining its profiles and dates together. The seed is 20261006. Intervals describe these evaluated model sets and are not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The 65/120 beat rate describes the fixed evaluation grid; its cells share models and market windows. Allocation and profile-change intervals resample models with their dates and profiles retained. Table 14 applies Benjamini–Hochberg correction to its three Spearman association tests.

Appendix D QA Dataset and Results

D.1 Dataset Statistics

The QA dataset contains 6,269 pairs across seven templates (Figure 12): T1–T5 each have 1,000 samples, while T6 and T7 have 778 and 491. T7 has no training split because its adaptive allocation labels are reserved for validation and testing. T6 has balanced labels: 50/50 rebalance versus hold.

Figure 11 shows the regime composition. Sideways markets dominate every template (>>65%), matching the empirical prevalence of range-bound periods. T1–T5 share nearly identical regime proportions because they sample from the same date pool; T7 raises the bull-market share to 29% so that its adaptive allocation task has adequate coverage of non-sideways regimes.

The amount of textual context increases with template complexity (Figure 13). L1 templates (T1–T3) include news or SEC filings in 71–75% of samples at roughly 2,800–3,000 characters; L2 (T4) is intermediate; and L3–L4 (T5–T7) reach 100% coverage at 4,500–7,388 characters. T7 provides the longest contexts (7,388 chars), combining news and macro signals for regime-aware allocation. Overall, 85.3% of pairs carry textual context, with a mean length of 3,997 characters. Context coverage and length rise with complexity: partial coverage in T1–T3, complete in T5–T7.

D.2 Full QA Results

Table 6 reports QA results: per-template mean scores with full information (T1–T7), the restricted condition without the covariance matrix (T4r, T5r), formula-focused allocation versus broader-task averages (F = mean of T4+T5; B = mean of T1+T2+T6+T7; T3 excluded as eight of ten models exceed 0.94), and mean scores by market regime.

The overall QA score ranges from .511 to .819. The widest template spreads occur on T3 (.336–.968), T5 (.230–.992), and T7 (.320–.843), while T4 remains near ceiling for every model. Aggregate QA rankings therefore combine tasks that differ substantially in both difficulty and the size of score differences between models.

We also recompute the QA average without T3 and T4. The resulting ranking has Spearman ρ=.988\rho=.988 with the seven-template ranking, and no model moves by more than one place.

D.3 T3/T4 Numeric and Structured Decisions

Table 6 shows near-ceiling numeric scores: eight of ten models exceed 0.94 on T3 and every model scores at least 0.956 on T4. Both templates provide quantitative inputs for sizing or pairwise allocation.

We further evaluate four models on a separate set of 50 T3 and 50 T4 structured-decision items per model. Each output gives a plan, feasible set, and binding constraints. Field score averages correctness across these fields; exact match requires all fields to be correct. Table 7 shows high field accuracy for DB-2.0-Pro and the two DS-V4 models, with lower exact-match rates. HY3-Preview produces valid JSON for all 100 items but no exact matches; 39 T3 and 44 T4 outputs receive partial credit. Its errors span constraint propagation, arithmetic, table reading, and multi-field consistency.

For DB-2.0-Pro and the two DS-V4 models, mean field/exact scores are .947/.787 on T3 and .959/.820 on T4. Their 95% CIs are [.924, .968]/[.707, .860] and [.938, .976]/[.747, .880], respectively, from 10,000 item-bootstrap samples retaining all three outputs per sampled item. The supplementary tasks distinguish component accuracy from complete consistency across the selected plan, feasible set, and binding constraints.

D.4 Task Diagnostics

Information ablation.

T4 and T5 prompts expose the statistics used by their allocation formulas: T4 includes pairwise covariance and correlation, and T5 includes the mean vector and covariance matrix. The restricted prompts remove covariance and correlation from T4 and the covariance matrix and its header from T5, retaining the T5 mean vector. The difference Δ=scorefull−scorerestricted\Delta=\text{score}_{\text{full}}-\text{score}_{\text{restricted}} measures the change in mean task score when covariance information is supplied. Results: Table 6.

On T5, only the two DS-V4 models have Δ>0\Delta>0: DS-V4-Pro falls by 0.332 and DS-V4-Flash by 0.073 when the matrix is removed. The mean T5 score rises for the other eight models, from 0.006 for Qwen3.6-Plus to 0.430 for Kimi-K2.6; Kimi-K2.6 rises from 0.280 to 0.710. T4 remains near ceiling in both conditions, ranging from 0.956 to 1.000 with full information and from 0.961 to 1.000 without the covariance statistics. The T5 pattern shows that the supplied matrix can hinder answer generation, although the ablation cannot separate table parsing from numerical reasoning.

Pairing the archived full and restricted responses by model and item shows that 460/500 T4 scores (92%) and 360/500 T5 scores (72%) are unchanged. The aggregate ablation differences are therefore concentrated in a subset of responses. These counts retain every evaluated item, including zero scores.

Supplied-statistic allocation versus broader tasks.

We compare formula-focused allocation tasks (T4: minimum-variance allocation; T5: maximum-Sharpe optimization, both with covariance statistics supplied) with the broader set of return prediction, VaR estimation, rebalancing, and regime detection tasks (T1, T2, T6, and T7). T3 is reported separately because eight of ten models score above 0.94. The F and B columns of Table 6 report these descriptive averages for all models.

The mean T4–T5 score is 0.863, compared with 0.652 for T1–T2 and T6–T7. This 0.211 difference favors T4–T5 for eight of ten models. GLM-5.1 and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B reverse the aggregate pattern, with T6 scores of 0.882 and 0.564 versus T5 scores of 0.421 and 0.230. These averages reflect different information and scoring conditions.

D.5 QA and Portfolio Outcomes

We relate the seven-template QA macro-average to portfolio Sharpe across four market windows and three investor profiles. The comparison uses 3,500 responses from ten models, seven templates, and 50 common items per template.

Each period–profile association contains ten paired model observations. The same QA scores recur across settings, so 120 portfolio cells are not 120 independent QA observations. Table 8 reports Spearman correlations and percentile intervals from 10,000 paired model-bootstrap draws.

Correlations range from −.67-.67 to .83.83. QA scores are positively associated with Sharpe in the conservative and balanced 2015–16 settings, whose two unadjusted intervals exclude zero. The other ten intervals include zero. In 2024, the estimates are −.10-.10, −.08-.08, and −.42-.42. The correlations vary across periods and profiles. These descriptive comparisons motivate evaluating candidate systems on portfolio outcomes under the intended profile and decision schedule.
