Appendix F Pipeline Diagnostics

F.1 Stage-Reference Agreement

Table 12 reports all five stage scores and CEPS for each normal-period model–profile cell. S1/S2 compare outputs with trailing-return rules; S3 measures allocation similarity and class exposure; S4/S5 measure turnover and lookback risk-state agreement. The exposure and outcome columns in Table 13 assess the corresponding investment requirements directly.

F.2 Lookback and Ex-Post References

Reference allocations depend on the return information used to construct them. We therefore consider two complementary references: a lookback allocation based on information available at the decision date, and an ex-post allocation based on subsequent realized returns. They provide a decision-time view and a hindsight view of the same portfolio decisions.

We compare them on the same 330 decisions in the 2024 normal window, holding model outputs, eligible assets, reference buy signals, and profile constraints fixed. For the ex-post reference, the mean and covariance in Eq. 7 use returns after the decision date through the next decision date, or year-end for the final decision. Both references use the same optimization procedure. S3–S5 use the corresponding reference weights; all other scoring definitions, including the lookback risk sample for S5, remain fixed.

GLM-5.1 ranks first under both references, and the same three models occupy the top three places. Across all ten models, the profile-averaged CEPS rankings have Spearman ρ=.77\rho=.77, with several other positions changing. Mean S5 rises from .108 to .283, mainly because the reference VaR and drawdown estimates are closer to those of the model portfolios on the unchanged lookback sample. Five of the 33 ex-post references retain the feasible initial allocation under the optimization rule in Appendix C.2; these cases account for about half of the mean S5 increase. The two references thus identify the same leading group while showing how reference choice affects individual scores and ranks. The model portfolios’ realized returns and risks are unchanged.

F.3 Allocation Agreement and Exposure Compliance

Table 13 separates reference-weight similarity, class-exposure score, target-exposure compliance, and realized financial outcomes for all normal-period cells. Exposure compliance checks both profile inequalities at each decision.

F.4 Allocation and Turnover

The 330 normal allocations have mean total-variation distance .306 from EqW and .890 from the profile-constrained reference. The mean decision-wise ratio of model to reference turnover is .203, using the same pre-trade weights for both targets. Reference allocations hold 8–14 securities with maximum weights .24–.72. Model mean HHI is .0207; its reciprocal is 48.3, while the mean of the individual reciprocal HHIs is 55.9. EqW over the eligible securities has HHI 1/n1/n and nn effective holdings. Table 14 reports these allocation diagnostics and their associations with realized outcomes.

F.5 Allocation Changes by Profile

Matching each model and decision date, conservative-to-aggressive risk exposure increases by .175 and bond-plus-cash exposure falls by .162; distance from EqW increases by .070. Across the ten model-level financial pairs, volatility rises by .050 on average (nine positive changes), drawdown magnitude by .047 (eight positive changes), and Sharpe by .214 (nine positive changes). The mean aggressive-minus-conservative Sharpe differences are −.423-.423 in 2015–16, +.935+.935 in 2020, −.039-.039 in 2022, and +.214+.214 in 2024. Table 15 gives the paired changes and model-cluster intervals. Risk-asset exposure is the equity-plus-crypto weight used to assess cap compliance; bond-plus-cash exposure includes uninvested cash. The exposure response coexists with period-dependent financial outcomes.

F.6 CEPS Parameter Sensitivity

We vary λ∈{0,.05,.1,.2,.5}\lambda\in\{0,.05,.1,.2,.5\} and α∈{0,.25,.5,.75,1}\alpha\in\{0,.25,.5,.75,1\}, changing one parameter at a time while holding the other at its default (λ=.1\lambda=.1, α=.5\alpha=.5). We recompute CEPS for all 330 normal-period decisions, then average by model within each profile and across the three profiles. Figure 20 compares each ten-model ranking with its default ranking using Spearman ρ\rho and Kendall τb\tau_{b}.

Rankings change little across the tested settings with λ≤.2\lambda\leq.2: within-profile Spearman correlations range from .988 to 1.000. Across the full α\alpha sweep, they range from .964 to 1.000. The three-profile mean ranking is unchanged at λ=.05\lambda=.05 and at α=.25\alpha=.25 or .75.75. At λ=.5\lambda=.5, clipping sets 253/330 decision scores to zero. In the balanced profile, 93/110 scores become zero, creating tied model means and making the ranking depend on the few remaining positive scores. These results support ranking stability around the default penalty and across the tested S3 weights.

F.7 Stage Scores and Financial Associations

Table 16 links CEPS to realized outcomes within each profile. Under the aggressive profile, higher CEPS is associated with higher Sharpe (ρ=.85\rho=.85, 95% CI [.41,1.00][.41,1.00]), connecting stage agreement to risk-adjusted performance in this setting. The association is weaker for conservative (.21.21) and balanced (.09.09) portfolios, whose intervals include zero. Positive associations with volatility and drawdown magnitude show that the financial interpretation of stage agreement also depends on the risk taken by the portfolio.

Table 17 reports pooled associations and stress diagnostics. Across profiles, CEPS correlates positively with Sharpe (ρ=.587\rho=.587). Under the balanced profile, higher normal-period CEPS is also associated with a lower worst-window drawdown relative to the profile tolerance (ρ=−.818\rho=-.818, 95% CI [−.975,−.346][-.975,-.346]). These profile-specific associations support assessing stage agreement alongside risk-adjusted returns and stress resilience.

Full and core CEPS.

Table 18 compares full S1–S5 CEPS with S1–S3 core CEPS, averaging across profiles. Spearman ρ\rho is .66. GLM-5.1 moves from core rank 4 to full rank 1, while HY3-Preview moves from 2 to 8. S4 turnover agreement and S5 risk-state agreement change the ordering of models with similar upstream scores.

Stress-gate threshold.

Rescaling each profile tolerance by .8.8, .9.9, 1.11.1, and 1.21.2 changes 27 of 360 scenario-level tolerance checks (7.5%). Most checks remain unchanged.

F.8 Paired Stage Interventions

Protocol and scoring.

Callable S4 selects order type, urgency, and slippage limits for a bound S3 target. Its score weights legality, target tracking, direction consistency, and cost awareness by .20, .35, .25, and .20; the runtime binds the target quantities and directions. Callable S5 selects a risk action from executed weights and risk statistics. Its reference chooses a 0.8 scale-down for a VaR or drawdown breach, equal-weight rebalancing for a drift breach, and hold otherwise. These scores assess plan choices under the bound task interfaces.

The balanced-profile intervention diagnostic uses callable S4/S5 plan tasks, so its downstream changes measure responses in generated execution and risk plans. The main ranking evaluates turnover and lookback risk-state agreement. The normal diagnostic covers 99 securities. The financial replay uses the tradable set defined in Appendix C.4. The replaced stage receives its reference output and scores one; downstream scores use the model outputs for those stages.

The paired analysis contains 300 intervention episodes: 110 normal and 190 stress. Replacing each stage with its reference output yields 1,500 branches and 4,500 stage-score changes. All 3,000 calls to subsequent model-dependent stages meet the required output formats. Confidence intervals for the complete matrices use 10,000 circular moving-block bootstrap samples within model–window units, and pp-values use Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control within each split. For this paired intervention analysis, S3 scores are recomputed from the stage allocations. Ten terminal-period S3 scores use only the finite correlation pairs, with the corresponding weights renormalized.

Figure 21 shows the stage-specific changes. Replacing S1 raises S2 by +.626+.626 in normal episodes, yet its mean effect on S3 is only +.017+.017 and is negative in 40 episodes. Replacing S2 raises S3 by +.023+.023 in normal episodes, with 39 negative cases. Under stress, replacing S2 or S3 lowers S5 by −.059-.059 and −.056-.056, respectively. Most changes at later measured stages are zero. Reference replacements improve some downstream stage scores, with effects that vary by stage and market condition.

Tables 19 and 20 report the complete cell-level means, confidence intervals, sign counts, and FDR-adjusted tests for the normal and stress episodes.

Callable-stage results.

Table 21 reports plan scores, outcome scores, and their components over 330 normal and 570 stress episodes across all three profiles. Runtime binding fixes S4 legality, target tracking, and direction, which carry 80% of the plan score; model variation is concentrated in cost awareness. Under stress, S5 action choice falls from .927 to .884 and adjustment scale from .917 to .857. These experiments evaluate model-selected execution settings and risk actions under fixed order and portfolio inputs.

Downstream gains and representative cases.

Table 22 excludes the directly replaced stage and retains positive, unchanged, and negative downstream means. S1 replacement improves the downstream mean in 109/110 normal and 186/190 stress episodes; later replacements have more mixed effects. To show what the measured changes mean, Table 23 selects the normal-period branch nearest the median within each sign group over S1–S3 replacements. Selection uses the same fixed rule for all models.

For HY3-Preview on September 2, replacing S1 raises S2 by .566 and changes S4 from a market to a limit order, gaining .100, despite a .116 decline at S3. Its S5 action changes from rebalance to hold while remaining correct for the respective input state. For DS-V4-Flash on April 1, replacing S3 gains .696 locally, but both downstream plan scores remain at their ceiling; the order type remains limit and the risk action remains rebalance. For the same model on October 1, replacing S2 gains .747 locally and .017 at S3, but S4 changes from limit to market and loses .100; S5 changes from hold to rebalance without changing its score. These cases show why both stage scores and action traces matter: changed decisions need not change scores, and large local score gains need not raise the downstream mean.

F.9 Within-Class Correlation Risk

Decisions and covariance estimates.

We use all 330 normal-period allocations: ten models, three profiles, and eleven monthly decisions from February through December 2024. We use the financial replay’s eligible securities, with excluded weight held in uninvested cash. For each security, we take its last 60 available return observations in the 90 calendar days up to the decision date. The primary sample covariance uses dates observed for all eligible securities, giving each matched pair the same positive-semidefinite matrix. Annualized estimated volatility is σ^​(𝐰)=252​𝐰⊤​Σ^​𝐰\hat{\sigma}(\mathbf{w})=\sqrt{252\mathbf{w}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}}. Uninvested cash has zero variance.

Matched allocation.

Let Hc={i:c(i)=c,wi>10−10}H_{c}=\{i:c(i)=c,\ w_{i}>10^{-10}\} contain the held securities in class cc, and Wcsec=∑i∈HcwiW_{c}^{\mathrm{sec}}=\sum_{i\in H_{c}}w_{i} their combined weight. The control assigns w~i=Wcsec/|Hc|\widetilde{w}_{i}=W_{c}^{\mathrm{sec}}/|H_{c}| for i∈Hci\in H_{c}, with all other security weights zero and uninvested cash unchanged. This preserves selected securities and total class exposure, including the cash-equivalent sleeve. The relative volatility reduction for decision ee is

re=1−σ^​(𝐰~e)/σ^​(𝐰e).r_{e}=1-\hat{\sigma}(\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{e})/\hat{\sigma}(\mathbf{w}_{e}). (17)

We report the arithmetic mean across 330 pairs and a 95% interval from 10,000 model-cluster bootstrap samples. The uniform weights are determined by the held securities and their class totals.

Variance decomposition.

With c⁡(i)c(i) denoting security ii’s class,

V⁡(𝐰)\displaystyle V(\mathbf{w}) =D⁡(𝐰)+I⁡(𝐰)+C⁡(𝐰),\displaystyle=D(\mathbf{w})+I(\mathbf{w})+C(\mathbf{w}), (18)
D⁡(𝐰)\displaystyle D(\mathbf{w}) =∑iwi2​Σ^i​i,\displaystyle=\sum_{i}w_{i}^{2}\hat{\Sigma}_{ii}, (19)
I⁡(𝐰)\displaystyle I(\mathbf{w}) =∑i<jc⁡(i)=c⁡(j)wi​wj​Σ^i​j,\displaystyle=2\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i<j\\ c(i)=c(j)\end{subarray}}w_{i}w_{j}\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}, (20)
C⁡(𝐰)\displaystyle C(\mathbf{w}) =∑i<jc⁡(i)≠c⁡(j)wi​wj​Σ^i​j.\displaystyle=2\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i<j\\ c(i)\neq c(j)\end{subarray}}w_{i}w_{j}\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}. (21)

These terms represent individual-security variance, within-class covariance, and cross-class covariance. Taking model minus control and averaging gives Δ​V¯=1.3599×10−5\overline{\Delta V}=1.3599\times 10^{-5}, comprising 1.0386×10−51.0386\times 10^{-5} from II, 3.2017×10−63.2017\times 10^{-6} from DD, and 1.0762×10−81.0762\times 10^{-8} from CC. Within-class covariance accounts for 76.4% of the mean difference, individual-security variance for 23.5%, and cross-class terms for 0.1%.

For si=Σ^i​is_{i}=\sqrt{\hat{\Sigma}_{ii}}, volatility-weighted pairwise correlation is

ρ¯​(𝐰)=∑i<jwi​wj​si​sj​ρ^i​j∑i<jwi​wj​si​sj.\bar{\rho}(\mathbf{w})=\frac{\sum_{i<j}w_{i}w_{j}s_{i}s_{j}\hat{\rho}_{ij}}{\sum_{i<j}w_{i}w_{j}s_{i}s_{j}}. (22)

Unlike a class-average correlation, this quantity changes with the allocation among correlated securities inside a class. Its mean model-minus-control difference is .033 (95% model-cluster interval [.021, .046]), positive in 289/330 decisions.

Results and estimator sensitivity.

Mean volatility reduction is 8.5% (95% interval [5.3%, 12.0%]), with 271/330 positive reductions. Table 24 reports every model–profile cell. The median reduction is 7.1%; mean reductions are positive in 27/30 model–profile cells and on all eleven decision dates. The paired design holds the class score fixed.

Pairwise covariance estimation uses each pair’s overlapping observations in the same lookback window. It gives an 8.1% mean reduction (95% interval [5.0%, 11.5%]), with 270/330 positive reductions. Table 25 also reports controls that equalize across all eligible securities within each class, or across all eligible securities. All controls retain the original uninvested cash. Expanding within-class holdings gives a 9.6% mean reduction under the common-date estimator; equal weighting across all eligible securities gives 15.5%. The primary held-asset control isolates weighting at fixed asset selection and class exposure. The main analysis uses common-date covariance to remain positive semidefinite.

Representative allocation.

DB-2.0-Pro’s balanced allocation on November 1, 2024 holds 82 securities. Equalizing within-class weights at fixed holdings and class exposures lowers estimated volatility by 8.0% and reduces ρ¯\bar{\rho} by .074. Its largest positive pairwise covariance contribution is AVGO–NVDA, with correlation .765 and 2.00% of total portfolio variance. NVDA–XLK contributes a further 1.07%, with correlation .887. Both pairs contribute correlated risk within this broad portfolio.

Appendix G Real-Time Evaluation

As discussed in Section 3.6, historical evaluation can overlap with market information in model pretraining (Li et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025a). PortBench therefore includes a real-time evaluation mode: at each decision date DD, the model receives only information available through the previous market close.

Setup.

We run real-time evaluation with daily rebalancing from 2026-07-16 to 2026-07-31 (12 trading days) under the balanced profile for six models: HY3-Preview, Qwen3.7-Max, Qwen3.6-Plus, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GLM-5.1, and Kimi-K2.6. DS-V4 and DB-2.0 models were unavailable through their APIs during the run. Temperature and decoding settings match Section 3.1. Table 26 reports mean CEPS under the lookback S3 reference, and Figure 22 plots daily scores.

Kimi-K2.6 leads with lookback CEPS .420, closely followed by GLM-5.1 at .418. Figure 23 shows high S1 (.78–.82), lookback S3 between .561 and .604, and low S4 (.047–.163). HY3-Preview has mean lookback S5 of 0. Figure 22 shows sharp drops for Qwen3.6-Plus and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on 2026-07-17, while GLM-5.1 has the lowest day-level variation (std. .020). Daily scores vary across models and dates, while turnover agreement remains low.

Scoring.

The lookback reference uses trailing observations available at the decision date. The daily results use a signal-constrained reference and total-variation weight scoring for S3. Historical portfolio comparisons use the profile-constrained lookback policy in Eq. 7. The twelve-day period, daily frequency, and six-model coverage complement the historical evaluation.

Appendix H Qualitative Examples

This appendix provides detailed examples of three core components of PortBench: the market base dataset (§H.1), the QA dataset (§H.2), and the five-stage evaluation pipeline (§H.3).

H.1 Market Snapshot Examples

A MarketSnapshot is the structured input constructed from the trailing lookback window and provided to the model at each rebalance date for the five-stage decision process. At each rebalance date, the model receives the snapshot through three isolated prompts and produces S1–S3; the sandbox then executes the S3 allocation and computes the S4/S5 execution and risk scores used in the ranking. The snapshot contains four structured layers: (1) per-asset price summaries with trailing returns and volatilities, (2) macroeconomic indicators, (3) a pairwise return correlation matrix with intra-class and inter-class aggregation, and (4) the current portfolio state. The two-layer correlation interface exposes within-class co-movement and cross-class hedging for joint allocation. Figures 24 and 25 illustrate these fields using representative assets from the six-class market dataset under contrasting conditions: a calm bull market (2024-03) and the COVID crash (2020-03). The field illustrations draw representative series from the full six-class dataset of 183 market series. Historical comparisons use the date-specific tradable subset in Appendix C.4; portfolio states are illustrative.

H.2 QA Dataset Samples

Figure 26 presents one representative sample from each of the seven QA templates (T1–T7), spanning complexity levels L1–L4. Each shows the context, ground-truth answer, and key reasoning step.

H.3 Pipeline Evaluation Traces

Figures 27 to 29 show complete five-stage traces for three models across normal and stress windows. Each trace reports a prompt summary, selected model outputs, reference targets, and stage scores. Scoring and execution use the eligible securities in each snapshot. Model outputs are shown as recorded. Their weights are normalized for execution, with excluded allocations held as uninvested cash; VIX appears as market context and any proposed VIX weight is held as cash. S1/S2 use the trailing-return targets, and S3 uses the profile-constrained lookback reference in Eq. 7. S4 applies the common next-close execution and cost policy, while S5 evaluates the resulting lookback risk state. The examples cover broad equity exposure, a large defensive reallocation, and a cash-heavy allocation.
